idiom_name: discriminated-union type with an exhaustive switch; zod discriminatedUnion at the boundary
implementation_notes: TypeScript absorbs the discriminator into the type system: a union whose members share a literal-tagged property is a discriminated union, and a switch on that tag narrows each branch (a never check gives compile-time exhaustiveness), so the classic base-class registry disappears - the type is the dispatch. Runtime safety comes from the boundary validator: z.discriminatedUnion reads the discriminator once and validates only the matching member instead of testing members in order, and falls back to a plain union when the discriminator key is optional. A hand-written decoder table is still justified when tags map to constructors that are not schema-derived.
pitfalls: Types are erased: annotating the parsed value as Event proves nothing, so without a runtime validator a payload carrying any tag still type-checks - parse at the boundary and treat the tag as untrusted.
A regular z.union tests members in order and returns the first match, which is where silently mis-bound payloads come from; z.discriminatedUnion needs a literal discriminator on every member.

Exhaustiveness is compile-time only: a switch without a default: assertNever(x) arm silently ignores new variants at runtime, and JSON.parse returns any, which disables the checking the pattern relies on.
